items.title: Commission preliminarily finds Temu in breach of the Digital Services Act for failure to tackle the sale of illegal products
items.summary:
Commission preliminarily finds Temu in breach of the Digital Services Act for failure to tackle the sale of illegal products Anonymous (not verified) Tue, 11/17/2026 - 11:11

The European Commission preliminarily found Temu in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) obligation to put in place reasonable, proportionate and effective measures to mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered on its platform.

The Commission preliminarily found that Temu's mitigation measures include ineffective controls to check the compliance of products; a weak content moderation system; and an ineffective sanction system.

Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, said:

Shopping online should not mean risking the purchase of illegal and unsafe products. Under the Digital Services Act, platforms are responsible for protecting users from the risk of illegal content and goods. The preliminary findings against Temu mark another step towards making the online world safer.

items.title: Commission hosts Apply AI Summit to boost Europe’s AI innovation and uptake
items.summary:
Commission hosts Apply AI Summit to boost Europe’s AI innovation and uptake Anonymous (not verified) Mon, 11/16/2026 - 13:43

Nearly 1,000 high-level policymakers, start-ups, industry leaders and researchers will take part in the Apply AI Summit in Brussels tomorrow.

They will discuss how artificial intelligence (AI) can boost Europe’s competitiveness across 10 strategic sectors and the public sector. The summit will also showcase concrete AI applications, European success stories and innovative projects. 

Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Technological Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, will host the summit and present the first Apply AI Startup Award to three European start-ups. The award recognises innovative European startups and scaleups developing AI solutions in the strategic sectors.

Alongside the in-person event, an online conference platform will run from 16 to 20 November, allowing additional 2,500 participants to join part of the summit.

The Apply AI Summit marks one year since the adoption of the Apply AI Strategy, which sets out how to speed up the use of AI in Europe’s key industries and the public sector. It concludes the first European AI Innovation Month, running from 14 October to 17 November 2026, organised by the European Commission in partnership with the Irish Presidency of the Council of the European Union.

items.title: Commission preliminarily finds TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed in breach of Digital Services Act for harmful ‘rabbit holes’ effect
items.summary:
Commission preliminarily finds TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed in breach of Digital Services Act for harmful ‘rabbit holes’ effect Anonymous (not verified) Fri, 11/06/2026 - 12:09

The European Commission has preliminarily found TikTok in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) for the so-called ‘rabbit hole effect’ of its recommender system.

TikTok's ‘For You' feed shows users a continuous stream of personalised videos, even when those are related to mental health struggles and body image.

The more a user interacts with a certain type of content, the more TikTok's ‘For You' feed algorithm recommends similar content. This design can be harmful when such endless and repeated exposure involves, for example, content about sadness, isolation or body image. These ‘rabbit holes' can have a detrimental impact on users' mental health, especially that of vulnerable adults and minors.

These preliminary findings focus on both risk assessment and mitigation measures.

items.title: Independent study on the impact of age assurance on fundamental rights and costs for businesses
items.summary:
Independent study on the impact of age assurance on fundamental rights and costs for businesses Anonymous (not verified) Wed, 11/04/2026 - 15:04

An independent study analyses the impacts of age assurance on fundamental rights and the costs for businesses concerned.

Age assurance is key for a safer online environment as it ensures that children only access online services and features that are safe and age appropriate for them. Nowadays, 1 in 3 children, aged 9 to 11 across 6 European countries, reports having a social media profile. Very few services are implementing age assurance in a systematic way.

To further strengthen the preparation of the proposed EU KIDS Act and the accompanying Staff Working Document, the European Commission procured a study to:

  • Analyse the impact of age assurance on key fundamental rights, including data protection and privacy, non-discrimination, freedom of expression and access to information;
  • Assess the potential financial impacts of age assurance on businesses, including micro and small enterprises.

The study was carried out by an external contractor. It does not assess the proposed EU KIDS Act and the compliance by any specific service provider.

The study's key insights are:

  • Fundamental rights – an age assurance framework can be both proportionate and respectful of fundamental rights. Interferences with those rights can be mitigated through appropriate safeguards. In particular, the framework should ensure:
    • Data protection and privacy – legislative coherence with the GDPR, high standards of privacy and security, and the development of technical standards;
    • Non-discrimination, freedom of expression and access to information – minimising friction for users, ensuring transparency, promoting user empowerment where appropriate through greater choice, and ensuring inclusivity and accessibility.
  • EU approach to age verification – the EU age verification blueprint can make an important contribution to the development of a coherent EU-level approach to age assurance. Specifically, the findings suggest that:
    • the blueprint has the potential to become one of the most affordable ways for service providers of all sizes to comply with age assurance requirements because it is privacy-preserving and open by design and its development costs have been publicly subsidised;
    • the roll-out of the blueprint across all Member States should be accelerated;
    • the provision and resourcing of effective fallback enrollment routes – including manual enrolment options at national and local level – should be ensured.
  • Costs for businesses – online services would inevitably face new costs. However, these costs are likely to remain modest for most services and to decrease over time, due to:
    • competition in the third-party vendor market,
    • the emergence of technical standards,
    • improvements in interoperability,
    • the availability of the EU age verification blueprint.
      • For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), the study suggests that it's unlikely to face excessive costs, thanks to affordable, ready-to-use age verification solutions and competition between providers. They will also benefit from having a common set of EU rules, rather than having to comply with different national requirements.

Read the study and its executive summary and the questions & answers on the proposed EU KIDS Act.

items.title: Call for evidence on advertising repositories
items.summary:
Call for evidence on advertising repositories Anonymous (not verified) Wed, 11/04/2026 - 11:10
  •   Opening: 04 November 2026
  •   Closing: 02 December 2026

The Commission is seeking feedback on upcoming technical guidelines concerning advertising repositories under the Digital Services Act (DSA).

The feedback is being gathered through a call for evidence.

The responses collected through the call for evidence will help shape guidelines aimed at ensuring that advertising repositories meet the needs of their users. Amongst other things, the guidelines will advise on:

  • how to make advertising repositories easily searchable
  • how to provide insights on how users are targeted and reached
  • how to make the content of advertisements accessible

Once adopted, these guidelines will aim to ensure that the advertising repositories provided by very large online platforms (VLOPs) and very large online search engines (VLOSEs) are effective and fit for purpose.

Effective advertising repositories are essential tools for enabling greater public scrutiny of online advertising. Transparency in advertising – revealing who pays and how citizens are targeted – helps to protect public health, ensure a high level of consumer protection and safeguard the integrity of elections. Advertising repositories also support effective supervision and enforcement of the DSA.

Next steps

The call for evidence will be followed by a targeted public consultation in 2027. Researchers, civil society, providers of VLOPs and VLOSEs and representatives from the advertising industry will be invited to share feedback on a draft version of the guidelines. The publication of the guidelines is planned for the second quarter of 2028.

Background

Under Article 39 of the DSA, providers of VLOPs and VLOSEs are required to maintain publicly accessible repositories of advertisements displayed on their services. These repositories (commonly known as ‘ad libraries’) provide information on the content of advertisements, who paid for them, the period during which they were displayed, how many users the advertisements reached, and the main criteria used to decide who saw the advertisements.

Article 39(3) of the DSA provides the possibility for the Commission to issue guidelines on the design of advertising repositories, following consultation with the European Board for Digital Services, researchers and the public. The guidelines will support the Commission’s supervision and enforcement of VLOPs and VLOSEs’ compliance with Article 39 of the DSA.

items.title: Commission accepts Temu's action plan to remedy the breach of the Digital Services Act
items.summary:
Commission accepts Temu's action plan to remedy the breach of the Digital Services Act Anonymous (not verified) Mon, 10/26/2026 - 10:28

The European Commission has accepted Temu's action plan to comply with the Digital Services Act (DSA) and tackle the availability of illegal products online.

Temu's plan focuses on five measures to remedy its breach of the DSA.

The company will carry out a platform-specific risk analysis. It will also use reliable metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of the mitigation measures put in place in reducing the risk of dissemination of illegal content.

The platform will assess the limitations of its content moderation and analyse whether, and how, its recommender systems may amplify the spread of illegal goods. Additionally, Temu will examine the influence of intentional manipulation and amplification of illegal items, including by sellers exploiting Temu's features to spread potentially illegal listings.

The company now has four months to conduct an interim risk assessment that covers a six-month period, until 30 November 2026, to ensure the implementation of the measures of the action plan.

The action plan is another example of how the DSA is enhancing consumer protection online and limiting the spread of illegal products in Europe. The action plan was submitted following a non-compliance decision in May 2026, in which the Commission found that Temu had failed to comply with its risk assessment obligations, and issued a €200 million fine.

Read more about Temu's corrective measures to terminate breach of the DSA.

items.title: Commission to investigate how Booking.com combats scams and fraud under the Digital Services Act
items.summary:
Commission to investigate how Booking.com combats scams and fraud under the Digital Services Act Anonymous (not verified) Wed, 10/21/2026 - 12:06

The European Commission has opened formal proceedings to assess whether Booking.com may have breached the Digital Services Act (DSA) by not having diligently assessed or effectively mitigated risks related to fraudulent listings and phishing scams.

The platform may also have breached the DSA when it comes to transparency because it did not clearly label as ads those listings whose providers paid for a higher ranking in search results shown to users.

The investigation will focus on the following areas:

  1. Fraudulent and non-compliant listings on Booking.com
  2. Phishing scams exploiting Booking.com's reservation and guest data
  3. Paid-for boosted listings not clearly identifiable as advertisements
